The '''Narva People's Republic''' (; ) is an unrecognised separatist entity that has been promoted through social media since 2022. It claims the city of Narva in eastern Estonia, where Russian-speaking residents constitute the majority of the population, as its capital.
The campaign emerged amid heightened tensions following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, drawing parallels to Russia's recognition of the Donetsk People's Republic and Luhansk People's Republic in 2022. Unverified accounts on platforms such as Telegram, TikTok and VKontakte began calling for Narva to break away from Estonia, circulating flags, arm patches and other symbols associated with a self-proclaimed "people's republic".
Estonian officials and local residents have denied any genuine grassroots support for the movement. Estonia's Internal Security Service (KAPO) has characterised the campaign as an information operation aimed at creating instability.
Background
Narva is Estonia's third-largest city and lies on the country's eastern border with Russia. Ethnic Russians make up approximately 95% of the city's population, and Russian is widely spoken as a first language. Following Estonia's restoration of independence in 1991, the city's predominantly Russian-speaking population faced complex integration policies, including language and citizenship requirements that left a significant portion of residents without Estonian citizenship.
Response
The Estonian government has dismissed the movement as a fabrication. In March 2026, KAPO issued a statement saying there was no evidence of any organised separatist activity on the ground, and that the online campaign bore the hallmarks of a Russian-directed influence operation. Local officials in Narva have similarly stated that no credible political group or public figure has come forward to support the idea of secession.
The Estonian Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not comment directly but noted that the country remains vigilant against hybrid threats. NATO and European Union officials have not issued formal statements on the matter, though the episode has been cited in policy discussions as an example of low-level destabilisation tactics.
